copy:
Bessel van der Kolk spent forty years building the most complete map of human trauma anyone has ever drawn.
He proved what happens inside a nervous system when a child grows up in an unsafe environment. He proved why talk therapy alone doesn't reach it. He proved why the body holds what the mind cannot process — and why, without the right intervention, it holds it indefinitely. His work became the foundation of every CBT protocol, every somatic practice, every EMDR session happening right now in every city on earth.
And then, near the end of his career, he said something the field is still catching up to.
"The body keeps the score. But understanding the score doesn't change it."
Read that again.
The man who spent forty years giving the world the language to understand trauma — who built the entire intellectual scaffolding of modern trauma therapy — is telling you that understanding it is not the same as changing it.
These are not the same process. They have never been the same process.
And once you understand why, something is going to click that explains everything. Why you can trace your hypervigilance back to a specific moment and still feel it fire. Why you know exactly what you're doing in a difficult conversation and still do it anyway. Why years of serious, committed therapy have made you the most self-aware person in any room you walk into — and you still brace before you walk through your own front door.
It's not you. It's not that you haven't worked hard enough. It's not that healing isn't possible for you.
It's that insight and integration are two completely different biological processes. And the entire self-help industry — including most of therapy — is built for the first one.
Nobody built for the second one.
Here is why that distinction changes everything.
Your nervous system is not a belief system. It is a survival system.
These two things run on completely different operating languages. Understanding — the insight, the click, the moment in session where a pattern finally makes sense — lives in your prefrontal cortex. In language. In the story you build about yourself, the connections you draw, the patterns you name. When something lands in therapy, that is your cognitive mind receiving information. That is real. That was worth every session.
But your nervous system doesn't live there.
Your nervous system lives in your body. In the part of you that starts bracing forty minutes before a hard conversation. In the part that reads a room before you've said hello. In the part that has been running a threat-detection program since childhood — scanning, preparing, performing safety for every room you walk into.
That part of you cannot receive information the way your mind does.
It cannot be told it's safe. It cannot update its threat assessment based on your understanding of where the threat came from. It has been doing its job — protecting you, brilliantly and exhaustingly — for decades. And it will keep doing it until it gets the one thing your understanding cannot give it.
Evidence.
Not information. Not insight. Not another session where something clicks.
Evidence. Repeated, embodied, accumulated slowly over time — the direct experience of showing up in a moment that used to feel dangerous and discovering, in your body, that nothing terrible happened. That the threat your nervous system has been preparing for since you were nine years old is not what it thought it was.
That is what changes the nervous system. Not the understanding of the wound. The repeated experience of approaching it, surviving the approach, and building — slowly, below the threshold of conscious awareness — a new set of facts for your body to operate on.
Van der Kolk called this the gap the field forgot to fill.
I spent eleven years watching that gap swallow my clients whole before I understood what was actually happening.
My name is Dr. M. Laurent. I'm a licensed clinical therapist. I've been in practice for eleven years and I want to tell you something I should have understood much earlier — something that changed how I work with every client I've seen since.

She could name her attachment style without pausing. She could trace every self-protective pattern back to the specific room, the specific age, the exact look on her mother's face that her nervous system had filed as threat and never unfiled. She had done CBT. EMDR. Somatic work. She had read every book, done every homework assignment, shown up every single week without cutting corners.
She was, by every clinical measure, one of the most self-aware people I had ever worked with.
She sat across from me and said: "I feel like I've been doing homework for six years and I still can't pass the test."
I started to say the thing I always say. She stopped me.
"Please don't tell me it takes time. I know it takes time. I know everything about why I'm like this. I just don't understand why knowing it doesn't make it stop."
I didn't have a real answer. I gave her the one I'd been trained to give. She left.

She knew everything. And she couldn't stop.

What is actually happening when someone understands their trauma with complete precision and still cannot make it stop? What is the nervous system waiting for that insight is not giving it?

Repeated, graduated, survivable contact with the truth — not the understood truth, the felt truth. The body needs evidence. Accumulated slowly, in doses it can metabolize, until it builds a new operating reality from the inside out.
Insight is Step One. It draws the map. It is real and necessary and cannot be skipped.
Integration is Step Two. It is learning to live in the territory the map describes.
My client had completed Step One more thoroughly than most people ever do.
Nobody had given her a tool for Step Two.
I went looking for one.
What I was looking for did not exist in any workbook I'd seen. Workbooks ask for insights — they want you to show your work, demonstrate growth, produce the articulate version of your inner life onto a page. That is more Step One. More performance. More audience, even when no one else reads it.

Something that would meet her wherever she actually was on a given morning — exhausted, shut down, ten minutes before the day started — without requiring her to be further along than she was.

She had always assumed it was just how her brain worked.

Approach and settle. Approach and settle. Small enough that nothing fired. Consistent enough that the body started updating.

Her daughter noticed before she did.
"Mom. You seem softer lately. Not weaker. Softer."
That is not a therapy result. Therapy is where she understood the wound. This is where the wound started closing. These are different processes. They always were.
She put it this way: "I spent six years understanding my wounds. It took about two weeks of these questions to start letting them close."
Not because she had a new insight. Because for the first time, she had the right tool for the right step.

"What would it feel like to stop performing okay — just for today?"

No streak. No date. No gratitude bypass that asks you to feel thankful before you've been honest. No shame for skipping — the journal is built for a dysregulated nervous system, which means it's built for the days when showing up is hard and the days when you can't get there at all. No audience. No right answer. No performance required.
Just you, and the parts of yourself you've spent years understanding, finally in the same room with nothing to prove.

You completed Step One.
This is Step Two.

I am going to say something that every woman who has spent years in therapy and still feels exactly the same needs to hear.
You are not treatment-resistant.
You are starving. While you eat.
And I know this because I am a retired therapist who spent 38 years watching women understand themselves completely. 
And then I watched my own daughter understand herself better than any client I ever treated. The same way. With the same result.
What she said to me in my kitchen last October still keeps me up at night.
Read every word of this. Before you decide this is just who you are now.
My name is Ruth Hollis.
I am 71 years old.
I retired three years ago after 38 years as a trauma therapist in Columbus, Ohio.
In those 38 years, I sat through more than 31,000 clinical hours.
I know what survival mode looks like. I have sat across from it for four decades. The bracing. The scanning. The woman who apologizes for crying in the one room built for crying.
I thought I knew why it wouldn't lift.
I was wrong.
I want to tell you about my daughter.
Erin was never my client. You don't treat your own child. But I watched her do everything right.
Nine years of therapy. Three good therapists — and I mean good, I checked, quietly, the way a mother with my training checks. Weekly sessions. CBT first. Then EMDR. Then a somatic program. She did the reading. She did the homework.
Two years in, something started going missing.
Not dramatically. Not overnight.
Just... less of her every year.
Not sadder. Flatter.
I noticed it on the phone before I noticed it in person. There's a sound a voice makes when someone is actually in the room with you. Hers was coming from somewhere farther back.
And here is the part that confused me for years.
She kept consuming. Ravenously.
Every book. The Body Keeps the Score, annotated in three colors. Podcasts on attachment theory at 1.5 speed while she ran. She could explain her fawn response at a dinner party and make it funny.
By any measure my field uses, she was doing the work. Her therapist told her the insight she'd built was remarkable. Everyone agreed she was doing the work.
And she was disappearing anyway.
She upgraded everything. A better modality. A weekend intensive. The workbook everyone recommends.
She kept flattening.
I kept a log without meaning to. Not in a notebook — in phone calls. What was missing from her voice this month that was there last year. When she stopped saying "I can't wait" about anything. When every story she told about herself started sounding like a case study.
I called a colleague. A trauma specialist I had known for 25 years. I described everything — without names.
"Ruth," she said, "it sounds like she's genuinely done the work. Her self-awareness is clearly exceptional. Sometimes..."
She paused.
"Sometimes this is just someone's baseline."
I drove home and sat in my kitchen for a long time.
Sometimes this is just someone's baseline.
I had said some version of that sentence to clients for 38 years. Healing isn't linear. These things take time. Be patient with the process.
I believed it every time I said it.
Then, last October, Erin stayed the weekend.
I came downstairs at 4am for water and she was at the kitchen table. Cold tea. Lights off. Sitting the way she sits — like the chair might be taken away.
I asked what was wrong.
And my daughter — nine years of therapy, three good clinicians, a bookshelf of understanding — looked at me and said:
"Mom, I can explain everything about myself. My attachment style. My triggers. Why I flinch when a text says 'we need to talk.' I'm fluent in it. I could teach a class on why I am the way I am."
Then she wrapped both hands around the cold mug and said the thing I can't unhear.
"And my chest has not unclenched once. In nine years. Explaining myself is the only thing I actually learned how to do."
And then, quieter:
"I've started to think maybe this is just who I am."
I stood in my own kitchen at 4am and I could not move.
Because I understood, in that moment, exactly what had been happening.
The flattening. The endless consuming that never satisfied. Fluent, and starving.
Those were not signs of someone who needed more time.
They were signs of someone taking in enormous amounts of understanding — and absorbing none of it.
And here is the part that destroyed me.
I knew the mechanism. It was in my training, decades ago, hiding in plain sight. I had simply never followed it to its conclusion.
The part of you that braces — that scans rooms, rehearses phone calls, keeps your shoulders somewhere around your ears — is not run by the part of you that understands things.
It's a survival system. Not a belief system.
Your thinking mind updates on information. You read something true, and it changes what you know — in an afternoon.
Your survival system cannot do that. It does not update on information. It updates on experience. Evidence. Small, repeated, lived moments of "I told the truth and nothing bad happened" — delivered in doses small enough to survive.
You can verify this yourself, tonight, against your own life. Find one thing you understand completely about yourself — the pattern you can name in real time, mid-conversation, while it's happening. Now check whether naming it has ever once stopped your chest from doing the thing.
That gap is not a flaw in you. That gap is the design.
And once you see it, you see what the entire shelf of healing tools actually is.
Books deliver understanding. Podcasts deliver understanding. Even the best therapy hour is, for most of us, fifty minutes of high-dose understanding — and a survival system in full brace can't absorb truth at that dose. It does what survival systems do with anything big and fast: it defends. She walks out with a better explanation and the same chest.
The label says healing.
The vocabulary says progress.
But almost none of it reaches the part of her that's actually running the show.
And if she's been gratitude journaling — which I recommended for years, because I believed it helped — it may be worse than nothing. Forcing a silver lining onto a nervous system in survival mode teaches it, one more time, that the truth is not safe to say out loud. It takes the little that might have landed and carries it out.
Now I have to tell you the part I am most ashamed of.
In 38 years of practice, I assessed everything. Symptoms. History. Cognition. Insight — we grade insight, informally, constantly. "She has excellent insight" is a compliment in my field.
Not once — not one time in 38 years — did I ask the only question that mattered:
Is any of this reaching her body?
There is no intake form for it. No box to check. We measure what a woman knows about herself. Nobody measures what her body believes.
I never measured it. Not once. In 38 years.
I told women "healing isn't linear" for four decades.
Some of them were healing.
Some of them were starving. In weekly sessions. Doing everything right. Fluent.
And starving.
Now I need to address what you're thinking, because I would be thinking it too.
You're thinking: my therapist says I'm making progress.
You probably are. Hear me clearly, because this matters more than anything else on this page: therapy is not the problem. Therapy built the map. Erin's therapists were good. The map is real and it is worth every session it took to draw.
But a map is information.
And you now know which part of you doesn't run on information.
The map was never supposed to be the whole treatment. It was supposed to have a second half. For most of us, nobody ever handed it over — because the second half isn't more understanding, and more understanding is the only thing the entire industry knows how to sell.
After that night in October, I spent six weeks reading everything I could find on how a survival system actually learns safety. Not how we explain trauma — how a body un-learns bracing. The literature is remarkably consistent: graduated exposure. Titration. Small survivable doses of the hard thing, repeated, with recovery in between. It is how every lasting nervous-system change ever documented actually happens.
Then I did something I'd never done in 38 years of recommending journals to clients.
I actually audited them.
I bought the popular ones. I went through them the way I'd assess a treatment plan for the most hypervigilant woman on my caseload.
Almost all of them failed.
The bestselling one is built on a daily streak. For a woman in survival mode, a streak is not motivation — it's a performance review. Miss two days and the tool itself is now one more thing she's failing at.
The dated ones are worse. A pre-printed date on an empty page is an accusation.
The gratitude-based ones ask her to perform "okay" on paper. You already know what that trains.
And the blank notebook — the free option, the one everyone tries first — hands a hypervigilant mind an empty stage and an audience of one merciless critic. Ask her how that went.
Every one of these looks like the same tool. They are not the same tool. One kind asks her body to absorb something. The others ask her to perform something. The label says journaling either way.
One journal passed.
It's called Back to You. It was built by people who clearly started from the same mechanism I've just walked you through, because every structural choice matches it:
No streaks. No dates. Skip a week — skip a month — and nothing on the page accuses you. It works anyway, because the sequence is waiting where you left it, and the sequence is the entire point.
No gratitude scripts. No audience. It never asks you to perform okay.
Just 365 prompts, sequenced the way a survival system actually updates — starting at doses a braced body can tolerate, deepening at the pace the research says lasting change happens. Small, survivable contact with true things.
The opening page says: "You don't have to do this perfectly. You just have to show up."
The early pages ask things like: "When did 'I'm fine' become your automatic response?"
And months in — only once your system has hundreds of small proofs that the page is safe — it asks things like: "What part of yourself did you hide to be accepted?"
Notice what none of these prompts ask. They don't ask you to understand more. You're done understanding. They ask your body, in small doses, to experience telling the truth and surviving it.
I gave it to Erin in November.
I am not going to tell you there was a breakthrough, because there wasn't, and if you've read this far you already distrust breakthroughs. What happened was smaller than that, and it was real.
The first thing I noticed — sometime in the winter — was that she stopped narrating herself. Fewer case studies at dinner. She'd just tell me about her day, like a person who was in it.
She told me the first real sign on her end was this: she wrote an answer one night and closed the journal without rereading it to check how it sounded. Thirty-four years old, and it was the first time she'd ever said something true without editing it for an audience. Nobody had ever asked her to do that in small enough doses before.
And in March, on an ordinary Saturday, she fell asleep on my couch in the middle of the afternoon.
She had not done that since she was fifteen.
Hypervigilant people do not fall asleep in other people's houses. If you are one, you know exactly what that detail means. There is no vocabulary of progress for it. There's just a body that stopped guarding the door.
I see the posts every week now. I know what I'm looking at.
"I know exactly why I'm like this and it still doesn't change anything."
"I can name my triggers in real time. Naming them doesn't stop them."
"Four years of therapy. My therapist says I'm doing the work. So why am I still rehearsing phone calls to schedule a dentist appointment?"
"I understand my childhood completely. My shoulders haven't come down since 2019."
You did not fail.
You tried everything the system handed you. The sessions. The books. The gratitude journal someone gave you with love. All of it.
But the system only ever handed you one half of the treatment. It measured your insight and called it progress, and nobody — including people like me, for 38 years — ever checked whether any of it was reaching your body.
Because there's no billing code for that. No one profits from telling you that the missing piece costs less than a copay and lives on your nightstand.
I am telling you now.
One page. A few minutes. Whenever you pick it up — the journal does not care when.
Give it six weeks. The first sign will not be a feeling. The first sign is behavioral: you'll write something true and close the book without rereading it. That's the moment you'll know something is finally being absorbed instead of performed.
The journal is $39.95 for the full 365 days. That's eleven cents a day — less than one therapy copay for an entire year of the half nobody gave you.
And it carries the guarantee I wish my field could offer: 30 days, and if it doesn't feel different, you don't pay.
I am not promising you a transformation. I'm suspicious of the word, and so are you.
I am promising you the half of the map you were never handed. Before you sign off on the conclusion my daughter almost signed at my kitchen table.

My A1C was 7.4. My new doctor called my old doctor "negligent." My old doctor had been the only one who listened to me for thirty two years. Now I had a prescription I didn't want, a doctor I didn't trust, and a medical record that said "non compliant" next to my name.
Dr. Whitfield's retirement letter came on a Tuesday.
Standard form letter. "After 38 years of practice, I'm stepping away effective March 1st. Your care will be transferred to Dr. Lauren Caldwell."
I sat at the kitchen table staring at it.
Thirty two years. I'd been seeing Dr. Whitfield for thirty two years.
He knew my history, knew my father's reaction to Metformin, knew my fear of medication, and he'd always worked with me, always said the same thing, "let's keep monitoring it, Mark, we'll try the lifestyle approach first, you're doing the right things."
Now he was gone.
My first appointment with Dr. Caldwell was March 14th. Routine physical. Transfer of records. Meet the new doctor.
I sat in the exam room, same room I'd been in for decades, same posters about heart disease and diabetes, different doctor.
Dr. Caldwell walked in. Young. Maybe 36. Laptop in hand.
"Mr. Bellamy." Firm handshake. All business. "I've been going through your file."
She sat down, pulled up my records, scrolled, and her expression changed.
"Your blood sugar history." She turned the screen toward me. "2022, A1C 6.1. 2023, A1C 6.5. 2024, A1C 6.9. 2025, A1C 7.2. Today, A1C 7.4. Fasting glucose 174."
She looked at me. "Five years of progressively worsening glycemic control. A1C above 6.5 for the last three years. No medication prescribed."
"Dr. Whitfield and I had a plan, lifestyle changes, diet, exercise, he was monitoring..."
"For five years?" Her voice was sharp. "Mr. Bellamy, your A1C has been in the diabetic range for three years without treatment. I don't know what your previous doctor was thinking, but this should have been addressed aggressively years ago."
My stomach dropped. "Dr. Whitfield knew my history, my father had terrible reactions to..."
"Your father's history doesn't change your A1C numbers, fasting glucose 174, you could be looking at neuropathy, kidney damage, cardiovascular events." She was already typing. "We're starting Metformin. 1000 milligrams twice daily."
"I'd rather..."
"This isn't a discussion. Your blood sugar is dangerous. If you refuse treatment, I'm required to document it in your chart as non compliance against medical advice."
The printer hummed. She handed me the prescription.
"Follow up in twelve weeks. We'll do another A1C and assess your response."
She stood. Left the room.
The whole appointment took fourteen minutes.
I sat there holding the prescription, hands shaking, the words "against medical advice" and "non compliance" rolling through my head like a verdict.
In the parking lot, I called my wife Diane.
"How was the new doctor?"
"She says Dr. Whitfield should have put me on Metformin years ago, and she wants me on it immediately."
Silence. "What?"
"She said five years without medication was irresponsible."
"But Dr. Whitfield always said you were..."
"I know what he said. She doesn't care. I either take the medication or it goes in my record that I refused."
That night I couldn't sleep, just lying in bed staring at the ceiling, Diane's breathing steady next to me.
Dr. Whitfield had respected my concerns, we'd worked together for over three decades, dietary changes, exercise, cutting refined carbs, daily walks, regular bloodwork every six months.
My A1C had climbed, yes, but gradually, no sudden spikes, no symptoms, no emergencies.
Was he wrong to be patient?
Was I walking around with damage building underneath and didn't even know it?
At 3 AM I went downstairs, sat at the kitchen table with my laptop, and started searching.
is A1C 7.4 dangerous
high blood sugar risks without Metformin
heart attack risk Type 2 diabetes men 50s
Every article said the same thing. Increased risk. Vascular damage. Neuropathy. Kidney disease. Cardiovascular events.
Maybe Dr. Caldwell is right, I thought, maybe I've been reckless.
But then I searched, Metformin side effects long term.
GI distress. Chronic fatigue. B12 depletion. Brain fog. Peripheral neuropathy. Increased fall risk in older adults.
And my father's face flashed in my mind.
He'd been on Metformin for fifteen years, started right after his diagnosis, the same medication sitting on my counter right now, and the GI issues came within six weeks, not occasional discomfort, constant cramping and urgency that ruled his life, made him afraid to leave the house, made him plan every outing around bathroom proximity.
They added Glipizide and the GI eased slightly, but then the fog rolled in.
He started forgetting things, small things at first, where he'd put his keys, what he'd gone to the store for, then bigger things, names of people he'd known for years, the punch line of a story he'd told a hundred times.
And the fatigue, that was the worst.
This was a man who coached my wrestling team, built our front porch with his own hands, fixed the car in the driveway on weekends.
By 65, he was napping twice a day, couldn't follow a conversation without losing the thread, lost interest in everything he used to love, just existing, going through the motions of a life that didn't feel like his anymore.
The tingling in his feet started at 67. By 69 he was using a cane because his balance was off. The doctor said it was B12 depletion from the Metformin, prescribed B12 shots, but the damage to his nerves was already done.
My mother said it was like watching him disappear.
He died at 71. Cardiac event. While taking the medications that were supposed to protect him.
Fifteen years of side effects. Fifteen years of feeling like a shadow of himself.
And it didn't save him.
I closed the laptop, rubbed my face, and just sat there in the kitchen with the prescription on the counter mocking me from across the room.
I didn't fill it.
One week passed. Then two.
Dr. Caldwell's office called. "Mr. Bellamy, our records show you haven't filled your prescription, Dr. Caldwell wants to confirm you're taking your medication as directed."
"I need more time to think about it."
"Sir, Dr. Caldwell noted this as urgent, she strongly recommends..."
"I said I need more time."
I hung up.
Diane found me in the garage that evening. "Mark. Talk to me."
"I'm looking for options."
"Options? The doctor said your blood sugar is dangerous."
"She said Dr. Whitfield was wrong for not putting me on Metformin, but Dr. Whitfield knew me for thirty two years, he knew my father's history, he saw what those medications did to him, he was being careful with me."
"But what if she's right? What if you..." Her voice broke. "I can't lose you."
"You won't. I just need to find another way."
"What other way?"
I didn't have an answer.
That weekend I searched everything. Berberine. Cinnamon. Chromium. Apple cider vinegar. Alpha lipoic acid. Every natural blood sugar supplement with actual research behind it.
I tried the top rated berberine on Amazon, six weeks, every morning without fail.
A1C check came back at 7.3. Basically unchanged.
Switched to high dose chromium, pharmaceutical grade, eight weeks, nothing.
Tried a full blood sugar stack from a specialty supplement store, berberine, cinnamon, chromium, alpha lipoic acid, the most expensive thing they had.
A1C 7.2.
Two tenths. Maybe three. Noise.
I was running out of time and running out of ideas.
Three weeks before my appointment I was back at my laptop at 2 AM going in circles, reading the same supplement forums, the same Reddit threads, the same dead ends.
Then I changed the search.
I stopped searching for supplements and started searching for the mechanism, why does blood sugar actually keep climbing in the first place, what's really happening inside the body when Type 2 progresses.
And I found something that changed the way I understood everything I'd been doing wrong.
It was in a metabolic physiology paper, the kind of thing that shows up when you stop searching "how to lower blood sugar" and start searching "what actually causes blood sugar to spike." Basic science. Not hidden. Not controversial. Just not something anyone had ever explained to me in a doctor's office.
The A1C number isn't the problem. The flood is the problem.
I read that line three times.
Your body has a pathway that controls how fast the food you eat turns into sugar in your blood. It's supposed to. When that pathway works, food comes in, the pathway breaks it down slowly, and sugar trickles into your blood gradually. Your insulin sees it coming and handles it calmly. Your numbers stay steady.
But that pathway is fragile. Stress wears it down. Processed food wears it down. Years of carrying extra weight wear it down. A little at a time, year after year, the pathway stops being able to do its job.
And then one day it can't control the speed anymore.

Dr. Whitfield had respected my concerns, we'd worked together for over three decades, dietary changes, exercise, cutting refined carbs, daily walks, regular bloodwork every six months.
My A1C had climbed, yes, but gradually, no sudden spikes, no symptoms, no emergencies.
Was he wrong to be patient?
Was I walking around with damage building underneath and didn't even know it?
At 3 AM I went downstairs, sat at the kitchen table with my laptop, and started searching.
is A1C 9 dangerous
high blood sugar risks without medication
heart attack risk Type 2 diabetes men 50s
Every article said the same thing. Increased risk. Vascular damage. Neuropathy. Kidney disease. Cardiovascular events.
Maybe Dr. Caldwell is right, I thought, maybe I've been reckless.
But then I searched starting insulin Type 2 side effects long term.
Weight gain, often significant. Blood sugar crashing too low, the shakes, the sweating, the confusion, people passing out, some not waking up from a low in their sleep. Testing and dosing built into every day for the rest of your life. And the part that stopped me cold, once you start insulin for Type 2, most people never come off it. The dose goes up, not down. It wasn't a fix. It was a door that only opened one way.
And my father's face flashed in my mind.
His diabetes drugs were the old kind, the pills, started right after his diagnosis, and the GI issues came within six weeks, not occasional discomfort, constant cramping and urgency that ruled his life, made him afraid to leave the house, made him plan every outing around bathroom proximity.
They added a second pill and the GI eased slightly, but then the fog rolled in.
He started forgetting things, small things at first, where he'd put his keys, what he'd gone to the store for, then bigger things, names of people he'd known for years, the punch line of a story he'd told a hundred times.
And the fatigue, that was the worst.
This was a man who coached my wrestling team, built our front porch with his own hands, fixed the car in the driveway on weekends.
By 65, he was napping twice a day, couldn't follow a conversation without losing the thread, lost interest in everything he used to love, just existing, going through the motions of a life that didn't feel like his anymore.
The tingling in his feet started at 67. By 69 he was using a cane because his balance was off. The doctor said it was a vitamin depletion from the medication, prescribed shots for it, but the damage to his nerves was already done.
By the end they had him on insulin too, on top of everything else, testing his fingers raw, a low one night that left him on the kitchen floor until my mother found him.
My mother said it was like watching him disappear.
He died at 71. Cardiac event. While taking the medications that were supposed to protect him.
Fifteen years of side effects. Fifteen years of feeling like a shadow of himself.
And it didn't save him.
His drugs were a different generation than the pen in my lap. But the pattern was the same. A medication that managed a number while the man underneath it slowly came apart, and at the end the number didn't matter because he was gone anyway.
I closed the laptop, rubbed my face, and just sat there in the kitchen with the prescription on the counter mocking me from across the room.
I didn't fill it.
One week passed. Then two.
Dr. Caldwell's office called. "Mr. Bellamy, our records show you haven't filled your prescription, Dr. Caldwell wants to confirm you've started your insulin."
"I need more time to think about it."
"Sir, Dr. Caldwell noted this as urgent, she strongly recommends..."
"I said I need more time."
I hung up.
Diane found me in the garage that evening. "Mark. Talk to me."
"I'm looking for options."
"Options? The doctor said your blood sugar is dangerous."
"She said Dr. Whitfield was wrong for not medicating me, but Dr. Whitfield knew me for thirty two years, he knew my father's history, he saw what those drugs did to him, he was being careful with me."
"But what if she's right? What if you..." Her voice broke. "I can't lose you."
"You won't. I just need to find another way."
"What other way?"
I didn't have an answer.
That weekend I searched everything. Berberine. Cinnamon. Chromium. Apple cider vinegar. Alpha lipoic acid. Every natural blood sugar supplement with actual research behind it.
I tried the top rated berberine on Amazon, six weeks, every morning without fail.
A1C check came back at 9.0. Basically unchanged.
Switched to high dose chromium, pharmaceutical grade, eight weeks, nothing.
Tried a full blood sugar stack from a specialty supplement store, berberine, cinnamon, chromium, alpha lipoic acid, the most expensive thing they had.
A1C 8.9.
Two tenths. Maybe three. Noise.
I was running out of time and running out of ideas.
Three weeks before my appointment I was back at my laptop at 2 AM going in circles, reading the same supplement forums, the same threads, the same dead ends.
Then I changed the search.
I stopped searching for supplements and started searching for the mechanism, why does blood sugar actually keep climbing in the first place, what's really happening inside the body when Type 2 progresses.
And I found something that changed the way I understood everything I'd been doing wrong.
It was in a metabolic physiology paper, the kind of thing that shows up when you stop searching "how to lower blood sugar" and start searching "what actually causes blood sugar to spike." Basic science. Not hidden. Not controversial. Just not something anyone had ever explained to me in a doctor's office.
The A1C number isn't the problem. The flood is the problem.
I read that line three times.
Your body has a pathway that controls how fast the food you eat turns into sugar in your blood. It's supposed to. When that pathway works, food comes in, the pathway breaks it down slowly, and sugar trickles into your blood gradually. Your insulin sees it coming and handles it calmly. Your numbers stay steady.
But that pathway is fragile. Stress wears it down. Processed food wears it down. Years of carrying extra weight wear it down. A little at a time, year after year, the pathway stops being able to do its job.
And then one day it can't control the speed anymore.
Food doesn't trickle into your blood. It floods in. The carbs in your meal that used to take 90 minutes to enter your blood now hit in 15. The flood arrives faster than your insulin can handle. You spike. Your pancreas panics and dumps a wave of insulin to catch up. That wave is too much. So an hour later you crash.
That alone would have been enough to keep me reading. But then I got to the part nobody had ever explained to me.
Every meal puts more stress on a system that's already failing, the insulin overshoots, your cells get a little less responsive to it, your pancreas wears down a little, and the next meal, the breakdown happens just as fast, but now your body is even less equipped to handle it.
A cycle that feeds itself.
I sat back in my chair.
Your A1C climbs not because of any one meal, but because every meal sends a flood your body can't handle, and the system wears down a little more each time.
That was why my A1C kept climbing.
That was why the berberine hadn't moved it.
That was why the chromium hadn't moved it.
That was why the lipid stack hadn't moved it.
Every single one of those supplements was aimed at the morning number, or at sensitizing insulin to handle the flood after it happened. None of them addressed the pathway that was letting the flood happen in the first place.
I was bailing water out of a boat while ignoring the hole in the hull.
That image hit me like a physical thing, because it was exactly what I'd been doing, real work, genuine effort, hundreds of dollars of supplements and months of disciplined dosing, all of it aimed at lowering a number while the actual mechanism driving the number ran unchecked.
And the insulin?
The injection they wanted to put me on would pour more insulin into my blood from the outside, forcing the sugar down, so the numbers on the chart would drop, Dr. Caldwell would be happy, but the pathway that controls the speed of the breakdown would still be broken, the flood would still hit every meal, the system would still wear down, and my body would lean on the outside insulin more and more.
The insulin would manage the number. It wouldn't stop the flood.
That's why the dose almost always climbs and almost never drops. That's why it's a door that only opens one way. You force the sugar down from the outside while the underlying system keeps breaking down, the same way it did for my father on his pills, his numbers looking fine on paper while the man came apart underneath them.

Papers showing pomegranate activates AMPK, a master metabolic switch, through a gentle mechanism that doesn't override the body the way the drugs do.

There's a fruit that's been used in Central Asia for over 5,000 years. The healers who used it back then didn't have a name for blood sugar. They didn't know what insulin was. They didn't have a way to measure what was happening inside the body. But they knew what they saw. People who ate this fruit daily had steadier energy. Calmer digestion. They didn't crash after meals. They didn't fall into the slow decline everyone else seemed to.
They called it the fruit of life.

Pomegranate contains compounds called punicalagins, one of the most powerful compounds your body uses to slow the breakdown of food into sugar back down to its natural pace. They restore the pathway that controls the speed of the breakdown in the first place. Not by forcing sugar down from the outside like the injection. Not in your gut like apple cider vinegar. Not by sensitizing insulin downstream like berberine. The actual pathway.
When the punicalagins are back in your system, the pathway has what it needs to do its job. Food enters your blood gently again. The flood stops. The spike eases. The crash eases. The pancreas stops wearing down three times a day. The cycle breaks. Your numbers come down. Not because something forced your body into compliance, but because your body finally has the raw material it's been missing.
The hole in the hull, sealed from the inside.
This wasn't fringe science, this was peer reviewed research sitting in metabolic and nutritional journals that nobody in a standard clinical setting was looking at.
I almost stopped there and ordered the first pomegranate supplement I could find. Bought a bottle off Amazon that weekend. Cheap powder capsules. Twelve dollars.
Diane saw the bottle on the counter. "Pomegranate? Since when do you take that?"

I took it for a week, didn't feel different, didn't expect to, you can't feel blood sugar moving without a meter, but I went back to the research and noticed something I'd skimmed past the first time.
The studies that showed results weren't using grocery store powder or juice. They specified standardized extract, verified concentration of punicalagins, low temperature processing, organic sourcing. One paper noted that heat processing, the standard commercial method for cheap pomegranate products, degraded the punicalagin content dramatically. The compounds that mattered were heat sensitive. The industrial process that makes pomegranate cheap also makes it therapeutically useless. The juice was even worse, mostly sugar, with the active compounds destroyed during pasteurization.
The Amazon bottle was ground up fruit scraps. Whatever had been in that fruit was gone before it hit the capsule.
That explained the failed week. It didn't explain the price I'd have to pay for the real thing.
At 4 AM I searched, standardized pomegranate extract organic punicalagins.
One brand kept coming up in the research oriented forums, people who'd clearly done the same deep dive I was doing, not wellness blogs, people citing studies, posting glucose readings, tracking month by month.
Alevia.

Week two, I woke up on a Saturday and the brain fog wasn't there, stood up from the couch without that slow getting started feeling, my thinking felt sharper, the food noise had quieted down.
Diane said something first. "You seem less heavy, like something lifted."
She was right. I didn't have a word for it until she said it.
Week four, I drove to a walk in lab, ordered my own A1C and fasting glucose panel, sat in the waiting room like I was waiting for a verdict.
The results came back the next morning.
A1C 8.2. Fasting glucose 168. Down from 9.1 and 215.

Almost a full point on A1C in four weeks. Without the insulin. Without any drug at all.

A1C 7.3. Fasting glucose 142.

Dr. Caldwell walked in. Opened my chart. Stopped.

Your body has a pathway that controls how fast food becomes sugar in your blood, and when it breaks down, food floods your blood every meal, and that's what damages everything underneath. I can email you everything tonight. I saved all of it."

copy:
There's a canvas beach bag on the top shelf of my hall closet that hasn't been unpacked since the 4th of July, 2019.
I know exactly what's in it. A pink and white striped towel from Target. A tube of sunscreen that expired 3 years ago. A pair of black flip flops with the arch worn down to a shadow. A paperback I never finished, a mystery set in Charleston that my daughter gave me for Mother's Day.
And a green tankini with a ruffle at the waist that I bought on sale at Belk in Bowling Green in June of 2019 and wore exactly one time.
I know it's on the top shelf because I put it there myself. Reached up, shoved it back behind the extra pillows, closed the door. It's been up there for 6 years and 4 months, and every time somebody's invited me somewhere with a pool or a beach or a lake, that beach bag on that top shelf is the first thing I think about, and it's the reason I've said no.
Last month my daughter Whitney called and told me my granddaughter Aubrey is being baptized at a beach house in Gulf Shores the second Saturday of July.
She said, "Mom, we rented the whole thing. 6 bedrooms. You get one. Everybody's coming. Ray. Trish and them. The cousins from Alabama. Aubrey wants you there. Please."
I said yes because I couldn't say no.
Then I hung up the phone, and I walked back to the hall closet, and I opened the door, and I looked at the top shelf.
And I stood there for probably 15 minutes.
My name is Marla. I'm 56 years old. I've lived in Bowling Green, Kentucky, my whole life, in the same little brick ranch off Nashville Road that my late husband Doug and I bought when I was pregnant with Whitney in 1993.
Doug passed in 2016. Heart attack in the driveway on a Tuesday morning at 6:20am. He was 54.
I've been the dispatcher at Sinclair Freight over on the industrial park for 22 years. I know every driver in a 200 mile radius. I know their kids' names. I know their birthdays. I know which ones haul reefer and which ones won't, which ones will pull double trailers to Louisville on a Sunday and which ones need Sundays off no matter what. I sit at that desk 5 days a week and I run 40 trucks and I do it well.
I sit is the part that matters.
I've been sitting for 22 years.
When Doug was alive I moved. He liked to walk. He liked to go to Lost River Cave and take the trolley and get out and hike the little trails. He liked driving over to Barren River Lake on Saturdays and putting our folding chairs by the water. He'd cook out on the deck 3 nights a week in the summer. He kept me on my feet without me realizing he was doing it.
When he died I stopped moving.
Nobody made me stop. I just stopped.
I went to work. I sat. I came home. I sat. I ordered supper from the Chinese place on 31W or picked up something from Cracker Barrel or ate a sandwich standing at the counter over the sink and then I sat on the couch and watched TV until I fell asleep. Weekends I sat and read. Sundays I sat at church and sat at Sunday dinner at Whitney's and sat at home in the evening.
For 9 years I have mostly sat.
I gained 34 pounds in the first 3 years after Doug died. My doctor, Dr. Kimble over at Graves Gilbert Clinic, told me at my physical in 2019 that my numbers were "creeping." She said my A1C was up. She said my triglycerides were up. She said my weight was up. She said "we need to think about this."
She sent me home with a printout about the Mediterranean diet and a pamphlet for a nutrition class the hospital offers on Wednesday nights.
I bought the tankini that week at Belk. I told myself I was going to lose the weight. I was going to walk. I was going to eat fish and vegetables like the pamphlet said. I was going to go on the annual family trip to Gulf Shores that summer and I was going to be different.
I went to Gulf Shores that year and I wore the tankini exactly one time, on the second day, on the beach at 8am when everybody else was still asleep, and I sat in a rented chair with a towel across my lap the entire hour I was down there, and I got up and walked back to the house before anybody could come find me.
I've refused to go back for 6 years.
I told Whitney the flight was too expensive. I told her the drive was too long. I told her work was too busy. I told her I didn't want to leave the neighbor's cat that I feed while she's at her daughter's on weekends. I told her a different lie every year and Whitney, who is 32 years old and has a job as a physical therapist and 2 little girls of her own, didn't believe me any of the 6 years.
She was patient with me until this year.
This year she said Aubrey wants me there.
Aubrey is 4. She calls me Grandmaw. She thinks I hung the moon. She's being baptized in the ocean by Whitney's pastor from her church in Louisville, and she wants her Grandmaw there.
There's no lie I can tell that's bigger than that.
So I said yes.
And I stood in front of the hall closet for 15 minutes.
And then I did what I always do when I'm scared, which is I called Delma.
Delma is my first cousin. Her mom was my mom's older sister. We were born 4 months apart. We were raised in and out of each other's houses in Warren County until Aunt Rose moved the family to Alabama when we were 11, and even after that we saw each other every summer for 2 weeks at my grandma's farm in Franklin, and we've been on the phone every 2 or 3 weeks for 45 years.
Delma is 58 now. She lives in Muscle Shoals, Alabama. She's a hairdresser at a salon on Woodward Avenue and she's been cutting hair for 36 years. Her second husband Cliff is a retired railroad man and they've got 4 grandkids and a bass boat and a little house on a corner lot with hydrangeas.
Delma has always been the bigger cousin.
I want to be plain about that because it matters to the story. When we were kids I was skinny and she was chubby. When we were teenagers I was chubby and she was heavier. When we were in our 30s we were both big women. Through our 40s and into our 50s we compared notes over the phone about our diets and our doctors and our numbers and our clothes not fitting. Delma had a bigger frame than me, always, but she'd carried more weight than me most of our lives, and we'd talked about it the way cousins talk about things, with love and honesty and no judgment.
The last time I'd seen Delma in person was Aunt Rose's funeral in Muscle Shoals in September of last year.
She'd looked the same as she'd looked for years. Big woman. Kind face. Struggled to get out of the pew.
I called her that night in April after I got off the phone with Whitney.
She answered on the second ring like she always does.
I said, "Del, Whitney's making me go to Gulf Shores in July."
She laughed.
I said, "It's not funny."
She said, "Baby, I know it's not funny. I'm sorry. Tell me about it."
I told her about the baptism. About the beach house. About Aubrey. About the tankini in the beach bag in the closet.
I told her I'd stood in front of that closet for 15 minutes.
And Delma, who has been my cousin for 56 years, was quiet on the phone for a long minute.
Then she said, "Marla, I've been meaning to tell you something."
I said, "What."
She said, "I've lost 18 pounds since Aunt Rose's funeral."
I sat down at my kitchen table.
She said, "I haven't told you because I didn't want to make you feel bad. And I didn't tell you at Christmas because I wasn't sure yet if it was going to stick. But it's stuck. 18 pounds. And I haven't changed my diet."
I said, "Delma."
She said, "I know how that sounds."
I said, "You haven't changed your diet."
She said, "Marla, I am eating the same things I've eaten since 1995. I ate biscuits and gravy at the Waffle House this morning. I had a Coke with lunch. I had Cliff's mama's pound cake on Sunday. I have not cut anything out. And I have lost 18 pounds since October."
I said, "How."
And Delma spent the next 40 minutes on the phone telling me something I had never heard before in 56 years of doctor visits and diet books and magazine articles and morning talk shows.
She said, "Marla, you know Miss Hazel? Comes in every Tuesday at 9:30 for her hair?"
I did know Miss Hazel. I'd met her at Aunt Rose's funeral. She was a retired home ec teacher who'd taught at the high school in Sheffield for 38 years. Little woman. Sharp. Always dressed nice.
Delma said, "Miss Hazel's daughter is a pharmacist over at the hospital in Florence. She's been on this thing for about 8 months and she'd been telling her mama about it. Miss Hazel told me about it in October, the week after Aunt Rose's funeral, and she said, 'Delma, I'm going to say something to you as a friend and you can throw me out if you want to. But my daughter has been reading the research on this thing and I think you ought to try it. I've been on it 3 weeks and my clothes are already fitting different.'"
Delma said, "I almost cried on her, Marla. Because in 36 years of cutting hair, nobody has ever said something to me like that. And I could tell she loved me. And her clothes really were fitting different. So I ordered it that Tuesday afternoon and I've been on it every day since."
I said, "Del, what is it. Just tell me what it is."
She said, "It's a supplement. Made out of the peel of a pomegranate."
I laughed. I couldn't help it.
She said, "I know. I laughed too. Miss Hazel didn't get mad. She said her daughter told her to keep an open mind. And she explained to me what it does, which is the part that mattered to me."
She said, "Marla, listen. You know how when we were kids we could eat a whole bag of Doritos and a Coke and a piece of cake and not put on a pound? Remember that?"
I did.
She said, "Our bodies were doing something back then that they're not doing now. There's a system inside you that controls how fast the food you eat turns into sugar in your blood. When it's working right, food comes in and sugar trickles in slow, and your body keeps up easy. Your body burns what it needs, and it doesn't have to store anything extra."
She said, "But that system wears down. Years and years, it wears down. Stress wears on it. Processed food wears on it. All the environmental stuff wears on it. Just plain aging wears on it. And every year it wears down a little more."
She said, "By the time you're in your 50s, that system isn't controlling the speed the way it used to. So the same biscuits and gravy you ate at 25 turn into sugar 4 or 5 times faster than they used to. Sugar floods your blood. Your body panics and stores it. Some of it gets stored as fat. And the rest turns into a spike, and then a crash, and then a craving 2 hours later that sends you back to the fridge."
She said, "It's not the food. It's the pathway."
I want to tell you something. When Delma said that phrase, "it's not the food, it's the pathway," I felt something in my chest let go.
Because for 6 years I have been standing in my kitchen at 8pm eating cheese and crackers straight out of the bag over the sink and hating myself for it. I have been counting calories on my phone and reading labels at Kroger and buying celery I never ate and Halo Top I only ate half of. I have been trying and failing and trying and failing. And Dr. Kimble had told me it was because I couldn't control myself. She'd told me to think about my choices. She'd told me to be intentional. She'd said all the things they say.
And Delma, my cousin, was telling me that a system inside me had worn down over years without me knowing it, and that the whole time it had been worn down my body had been storing sugar as fat instead of using it, and that the cravings that pulled me to the cheese and crackers were not because I was weak. They were because that system was broken and my body was crashing and reaching for whatever would spike it back up.

Dr. Whitfield's retirement letter came on a Tuesday.
Standard form letter. "After 38 years of practice, I'm stepping away effective March 1st. Your care will be transferred to Dr. Lauren Caldwell."
I sat at the kitchen table staring at it.
Thirty two years. I'd been seeing Dr. Whitfield for thirty two years.
He knew my history, knew my father's reaction to Metformin, knew my fear of medication, and he'd always worked with me, always said the same thing, "let's keep monitoring it, Mark, we'll try the lifestyle approach first, you're doing the right things."
Now he was gone.
My first appointment with Dr. Caldwell was March 14th. Routine physical. Transfer of records. Meet the new doctor.

Dr. Caldwell walked in. Young. Maybe 36. Laptop in hand.
"Mr. Bellamy." Firm handshake. All business. "I've been going through your file."
She sat down, pulled up my records, scrolled, and her expression changed.
"Your blood sugar history." She turned the screen toward me. "2022, A1C 6.1. 2023, A1C 6.5. 2024, A1C 6.9. 2025, A1C 7.2. Today, A1C 7.4. Fasting glucose 174."
She looked at me. "Five years of progressively worsening glycemic control. A1C above 6.5 for the last three years. No medication prescribed."
"Dr. Whitfield and I had a plan, lifestyle changes, diet, exercise, he was monitoring..."
"For five years?" Her voice was sharp. "Mr. Bellamy, your A1C has been in the diabetic range for three years without treatment. I don't know what your previous doctor was thinking, but this should have been addressed aggressively years ago."

"I'd rather..."
"This isn't a discussion. Your blood sugar is dangerous. If you refuse treatment, I'm required to document it in your chart as non compliance against medical advice."
The printer hummed. She handed me the prescription.
"Follow up in twelve weeks. We'll do another A1C and assess your response."
She stood. Left the room.
The whole appointment took fourteen minutes.
I sat there holding the prescription, hands shaking, the words "against medical advice" and "non compliance" rolling through my head like a verdict.
In the parking lot, I called my wife Diane.

"She says Dr. Whitfield should have put me on Metformin years ago, and she wants me on it immediately."

high blood sugar risks without Metformin
heart attack risk Type 2 diabetes men 50s

Food doesn't trickle into your blood. It floods in. The carbs in your meal that used to take 90 minutes to enter your blood now hit in 15. The flood arrives faster than your insulin can handle. You spike. Your pancreas panics and dumps a wave of insulin to catch up. That wave is too much. So an hour later you crash.

"Dr. Whitfield and I had a plan, lifestyle changes, diet, exercise, he was monitoring..."
"For five years?" Her voice was sharp. "Mr. Bellamy, your blood pressure has been in the stage two range for three years without treatment, I don't know what your previous doctor was thinking, but this should have been addressed aggressively years ago."

"Your father's history doesn't change your blood pressure numbers, 162/98, you could have a heart attack, stroke, kidney damage." She was already typing. "We're starting Lisinopril. 20 milligrams daily."
"I'd rather..."

is 162 over 98 dangerous

heart attack risk hypertension men 50s

copy:
There's a canvas beach bag on the top shelf of my hall closet that hasn't been unpacked since the 4th of July, 2019.
I know exactly what's in it. A pink and white striped towel from Target. A tube of sunscreen that expired 3 years ago. A pair of black flip flops with the arch worn down to a shadow. A paperback I never finished, a mystery set in Charleston that my daughter gave me for Mother's Day.
And a green tankini with a ruffle at the waist that I bought on sale at Belk in Bowling Green in June of 2019 and wore exactly one time.
I know it's on the top shelf because I put it there myself. Reached up, shoved it back behind the extra pillows, closed the door. It's been up there for 6 years and 4 months, and every time somebody's invited me somewhere with a pool or a beach or a lake, that beach bag on that top shelf is the first thing I think about, and it's the reason I've said no.
Last month my daughter Whitney called and told me my granddaughter Aubrey is being baptized at a beach house in Gulf Shores the second Saturday of July.
She said, "Mom, we rented the whole thing. 6 bedrooms. You get one. Everybody's coming. Ray. Trish and them. The cousins from Alabama. Aubrey wants you there. Please."
I said yes because I couldn't say no.
Then I hung up the phone, and I walked back to the hall closet, and I opened the door, and I looked at the top shelf.
And I stood there for probably 15 minutes.
My name is Marla. I'm 56 years old. I've lived in Bowling Green, Kentucky, my whole life, in the same little brick ranch off Nashville Road that my late husband Doug and I bought when I was pregnant with Whitney in 1993.
Doug passed in 2016. Heart attack in the driveway on a Tuesday morning at 6:20am. He was 54.
I've been the dispatcher at Sinclair Freight over on the industrial park for 22 years. I know every driver in a 200 mile radius. I know their kids' names. I know their birthdays. I know which ones haul reefer and which ones won't, which ones will pull double trailers to Louisville on a Sunday and which ones need Sundays off no matter what. I sit at that desk 5 days a week and I run 40 trucks and I do it well.
I sit is the part that matters.
I've been sitting for 22 years.
When Doug was alive I moved. He liked to walk. He liked to go to Lost River Cave and take the trolley and get out and hike the little trails. He liked driving over to Barren River Lake on Saturdays and putting our folding chairs by the water. He'd cook out on the deck 3 nights a week in the summer. He kept me on my feet without me realizing he was doing it.
When he died I stopped moving.
Nobody made me stop. I just stopped.
I went to work. I sat. I came home. I sat. I ordered supper from the Chinese place on 31W or picked up something from Cracker Barrel or ate a sandwich standing at the counter over the sink and then I sat on the couch and watched TV until I fell asleep. Weekends I sat and read. Sundays I sat at church and sat at Sunday dinner at Whitney's and sat at home in the evening.
For 9 years I have mostly sat.
I gained 34 pounds in the first 3 years after Doug died. My doctor, Dr. Kimble over at Graves Gilbert Clinic, told me at my physical in 2019 that my numbers were "creeping." She said my A1C was up. She said my triglycerides were up. She said my weight was up. She said "we need to think about this."
She sent me home with a printout about the Mediterranean diet and a pamphlet for a nutrition class the hospital offers on Wednesday nights.
I bought the tankini that week at Belk. I told myself I was going to lose the weight. I was going to walk. I was going to eat fish and vegetables like the pamphlet said. I was going to go on the annual family trip to Gulf Shores that summer and I was going to be different.
I went to Gulf Shores that year and I wore the tankini exactly one time, on the second day, on the beach at 8am when everybody else was still asleep, and I sat in a rented chair with a towel across my lap the entire hour I was down there, and I got up and walked back to the house before anybody could come find me.
I've refused to go back for 6 years.
I told Whitney the flight was too expensive. I told her the drive was too long. I told her work was too busy. I told her I didn't want to leave the neighbor's cat that I feed while she's at her daughter's on weekends. I told her a different lie every year and Whitney, who is 32 years old and has a job as a physical therapist and 2 little girls of her own, didn't believe me any of the 6 years.
She was patient with me until this year.
This year she said Aubrey wants me there.
Aubrey is 4. She calls me Grandmaw. She thinks I hung the moon. She's being baptized in the ocean by Whitney's pastor from her church in Louisville, and she wants her Grandmaw there.
There's no lie I can tell that's bigger than that.
So I said yes.
And I stood in front of the hall closet for 15 minutes.
And then I did what I always do when I'm scared, which is I called Delma.
Delma is my first cousin. Her mom was my mom's older sister. We were born 4 months apart. We were raised in and out of each other's houses in Warren County until Aunt Rose moved the family to Alabama when we were 11, and even after that we saw each other every summer for 2 weeks at my grandma's farm in Franklin, and we've been on the phone every 2 or 3 weeks for 45 years.
Delma is 58 now. She lives in Muscle Shoals, Alabama. She's a hairdresser at a salon on Woodward Avenue and she's been cutting hair for 36 years. Her second husband Cliff is a retired railroad man and they've got 4 grandkids and a bass boat and a little house on a corner lot with hydrangeas.
Delma has always been the bigger cousin.
I want to be plain about that because it matters to the story. When we were kids I was skinny and she was chubby. When we were teenagers I was chubby and she was heavier. When we were in our 30s we were both big women. Through our 40s and into our 50s we compared notes over the phone about our diets and our doctors and our numbers and our clothes not fitting. Delma had a bigger frame than me, always, but she'd carried more weight than me most of our lives, and we'd talked about it the way cousins talk about things, with love and honesty and no judgment.
The last time I'd seen Delma in person was Aunt Rose's funeral in Muscle Shoals in September of last year.
She'd looked the same as she'd looked for years. Big woman. Kind face. Struggled to get out of the pew.
I called her that night in April after I got off the phone with Whitney.
She answered on the second ring like she always does.
I said, "Del, Whitney's making me go to Gulf Shores in July."
She laughed.
I said, "It's not funny."
She said, "Baby, I know it's not funny. I'm sorry. Tell me about it."
I told her about the baptism. About the beach house. About Aubrey. About the tankini in the beach bag in the closet.
I told her I'd stood in front of that closet for 15 minutes.
And Delma, who has been my cousin for 56 years, was quiet on the phone for a long minute.
Then she said, "Marla, I've been meaning to tell you something."
I said, "What."
She said, "I've lost 18 pounds since Aunt Rose's funeral."
I sat down at my kitchen table.
She said, "I haven't told you because I didn't want to make you feel bad. And I didn't tell you at Christmas because I wasn't sure yet if it was going to stick. But it's stuck. 18 pounds. And I haven't changed my diet."
I said, "Delma."
She said, "I know how that sounds."
I said, "You haven't changed your diet."
She said, "Marla, I am eating the same things I've eaten since 1995. I ate biscuits and gravy at the Waffle House this morning. I had a Coke with lunch. I had Cliff's mama's pound cake on Sunday. I have not cut anything out. And I have lost 18 pounds since October."
I said, "How."
And Delma spent the next 40 minutes on the phone telling me something I had never heard before in 56 years of doctor visits and diet books and magazine articles and morning talk shows.
She said, "Marla, you know Miss Hazel? Comes in every Tuesday at 9:30 for her hair?"
I did know Miss Hazel. I'd met her at Aunt Rose's funeral. She was a retired home ec teacher who'd taught at the high school in Sheffield for 38 years. Little woman. Sharp. Always dressed nice.
Delma said, "Miss Hazel's daughter is a pharmacist over at the hospital in Florence. She's been on this thing for about 8 months and she'd been telling her mama about it. Miss Hazel told me about it in October, the week after Aunt Rose's funeral, and she said, 'Delma, I'm going to say something to you as a friend and you can throw me out if you want to. But my daughter has been reading the research on this thing and I think you ought to try it. I've been on it 3 weeks and my clothes are already fitting different.'"
Delma said, "I almost cried on her, Marla. Because in 36 years of cutting hair, nobody has ever said something to me like that. And I could tell she loved me. And her clothes really were fitting different. So I ordered it that Tuesday afternoon and I've been on it every day since."
I said, "Del, what is it. Just tell me what it is."
She said, "It's a supplement. Made out of the peel of a pomegranate."
I laughed. I couldn't help it.
She said, "I know. I laughed too. Miss Hazel didn't get mad. She said her daughter told her to keep an open mind. And she explained to me what it does, which is the part that mattered to me."
She said, "Marla, listen. You know how when we were kids we could eat a whole bag of Doritos and a Coke and a piece of cake and not put on a pound? Remember that?"
I did.
She said, "Our bodies were doing something back then that they're not doing now. There's a system inside you that controls how fast the food you eat turns into sugar in your blood. When it's working right, food comes in and sugar trickles in slow, and your body keeps up easy. Your body burns what it needs, and it doesn't have to store anything extra."
She said, "But that system wears down. Years and years, it wears down. Stress wears on it. Processed food wears on it. All the environmental stuff wears on it. Just plain aging wears on it. And every year it wears down a little more."
She said, "By the time you're in your 50s, that system isn't controlling the speed the way it used to. So the same biscuits and gravy you ate at 25 turn into sugar 4 or 5 times faster than they used to. Sugar floods your blood. Your body panics and stores it. Some of it gets stored as fat. And the rest turns into a spike, and then a crash, and then a craving 2 hours later that sends you back to the fridge."
She said, "It's not the food. It's the pathway."
I want to tell you something. When Delma said that phrase, "it's not the food, it's the pathway," I felt something in my chest let go.
Because for 6 years I have been standing in my kitchen at 8pm eating cheese and crackers straight out of the bag over the sink and hating myself for it. I have been counting calories on my phone and reading labels at Kroger and buying celery I never ate and Halo Top I only ate half of. I have been trying and failing and trying and failing. And Dr. Kimble had told me it was because I couldn't control myself. She'd told me to think about my choices. She'd told me to be intentional. She'd said all the things they say.
And Delma, my cousin, was telling me that a system inside me had worn down over years without me knowing it, and that the whole time it had been worn down my body had been storing sugar as fat instead of using it, and that the cravings that pulled me to the cheese and crackers were not because I was weak. They were because that system was broken and my body was crashing and reaching for whatever would spike it back up.
I sat at my kitchen table and I cried and Delma stayed on the phone with me.
She said, "Baby, I know."
I said, "How does the pomegranate thing help."

The crashes soften. The cravings settle."
She said, "Marla, I do not crave sugar at night anymore. I do not stand at my counter at 9pm eating fudge stripes out of the pack. I do not sit at the salon at 2 in the afternoon dying for a Coke. I eat the same things. I just don't want them the way I did. And my body is doing something different with them. That's the only way I can describe it."
She said, "And it's not just the weight. My energy is different. I did a full 8 hour Saturday at the salon last weekend and I came home and I cleaned my kitchen instead of collapsing on the couch. That hasn't happened since Cliff and I bought this house."
She said, "It's the peel, Marla. Not the juice. Miss Hazel's daughter had to look at 3 or 4 different brands before she found one that was actually made from the peel and standardized to the punicalagins. Most pomegranate stuff on the shelves at CVS is just juice, or it's standardized to something called ellagic acid, which is related but it's not the same compound. The brand her daughter found is called Auniva. It's organic pomegranate peel extract, made in the USA, 2 capsules a day. That's the whole thing."
I said, "Where do you get it."
She said, "Their website. auniva.co. There's a 90 day money back guarantee. If it doesn't do anything for you in 90 days, you send the bottle back and they put every penny back on your card. That's what let me try it. I had 90 days to lose and Miss Hazel sitting in my chair every Tuesday morning showing me it worked on her."
I ordered a bottle that night.
I want to tell you about the next 3 months honestly, because I'm 56 years old and I've been sold to enough times to know how these things go, and I want to be plain about what happened.
The bottle came in 4 days. Auniva's Pomegranate. Organic concentrated pomegranate peel extract. Standardized to punicalagins. Made in the USA. 30 servings per bottle. 2 capsules a day with breakfast. That's the whole product.
Week 1, I didn't feel anything.
Week 2, I didn't feel anything.
Week 3 was a Thursday afternoon and I was at my desk at Sinclair and I realized at 4:30pm that I hadn't been to the vending machine.
That sounds like a small thing. I want you to understand it wasn't. I have been to the vending machine in the hallway outside dispatch every single afternoon between 2:15 and 3pm for 22 years. I get a Diet Coke and a bag of Cheez Its most days. Sometimes a Snickers. It is the middle of my day. It has been the middle of my day since Whitney was in the 5th grade.
Week 3, Thursday, 4:30pm, I looked up from my screen and I realized I'd forgotten.
I hadn't decided to skip it. I hadn't fought a craving. I'd just forgotten it existed.
I didn't tell anybody. I went home. I ate supper. I went to bed.
Week 4 I dropped 3 pounds. Not on purpose. I noticed it on my scale in the bathroom on a Saturday morning. I stood on the scale and looked at the number and stood on it again to make sure.
Week 5 I skipped the vending machine 4 days out of 5.
Week 6 I went to Cracker Barrel with the ladies from work on a Wednesday night and I ordered the meatloaf plate the way I always do, and I ate about two thirds of it and pushed the plate away because I was full. I have not pushed a Cracker Barrel plate away in 20 years. Debbie Ann across the table said, "Marla, you feeling okay?" I said I was just full. She looked at me like I'd said something in French.
Week 7 my pants were loose in the waist.
Week 8 I stopped needing a nap on Sundays.
Week 9 I went to Belk on a Saturday morning in June.
I walked back to the swimsuit section, which is on the second floor next to the shoes, and I stood in front of the rack for 20 minutes.
I picked up 4 suits. I took them to the fitting room.
I tried on a navy tankini with a wrap style top and a swim skirt.
I looked in the mirror in that fitting room and I did not hate what I saw. I want to be careful how I say that. I did not love it. I am 56 years old and I've been a bigger woman for 25 years and I do not have the body I had at 30. But what I saw in the mirror at Belk was a woman who looked like herself again. Like Marla. Like the Marla Doug used to know. Like a person, not a shame.
I bought the suit.
I drove home. I put the Belk bag on the kitchen table. I called Delma.
She was in the middle of a color at the salon and she picked up on the third ring anyway.
I said, "Del."
She said, "Yeah baby."
I said, "I bought a swimsuit."
She got quiet.
Then she said, "Aw, honey."
Then she said, "Aw, honey."
And she stayed on the phone with me while I sat at my kitchen table and cried.
I went to Gulf Shores the second Saturday of July.
I drove down with Whitney and the girls in her Pilot. 8 hours. We stopped at a Cracker Barrel in Birmingham for lunch. I got a salad. Not because I was making myself. Because I wanted one.
Aubrey was baptized in the surf by Whitney's pastor on Saturday morning at 9am. She wore a little white dress that Whitney's mother in law had sewn. She stood in the water with the waves at her knees and her preacher put his hand on her head and she looked up at me on the beach and she waved.
I waved back.
I was wearing the navy tankini and a pair of denim shorts and a straw hat and I was standing in the sand with my toes buried and I was there. All the way there. Not sitting in a rented chair with a towel across my lap. Not planning my escape route back to the house. Just there. Watching my granddaughter get baptized.
Later that afternoon, after lunch, when everybody else was napping, I walked down to the water by myself. I took the tankini top off my shoulders enough that the sun hit my collarbone for the first time in probably 10 years. I stood at the edge of the ocean with the water washing over my feet.
And I stood there for maybe 20 minutes and I let myself be a woman on a beach.
That was 3 months ago. I've been on Auniva's Pomegranate 6 months total now. I've lost 22 pounds. I've not changed what I eat, which is the part that still surprises me. I've started walking after supper the way Doug used to. Just around the block at first. Now 2 miles most nights. I take my phone. I listen to podcasts about history. I come back and I sit on the porch for a while before I go in.
I have felt like myself for the first time since I was 47 years old.

It isn't you.
